extracted.intended_audience: college faculty, administrators, and curriculum designers responsible for undergraduate scientific courses
extracted.subtask_description: Prescriptive standards and recommendations for structuring undergraduate scientific courses of study so they are equivalent in rigor and purpose to classical curricula; covers admission requirements, curricular content, methods (laboratory/field), language and mathematics preparation, specialization, and textbook/teaching standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admission requirements equivalent to classical course
rubrics_metrics.description: For entry upon an ordinary classical course a student is examined in the 'English branches,' in Latin, in Greek, and in mathematics; for the scientific course we may properly demand the same English branches and mathematics, so that the question really is, 'What shall we substitute for the Latin and Greek?'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require substitution subjects such as French, German, chemistry, and physics (any two might be chosen). If these cannot be secured, acceptable substitutes include additional mathematics or Latin as a makeshift. The essential thing is that the candidate shall have spent as much time and done as much work in preparation for college as the classical student; for less than this no diploma should be granted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific courses must be equivalent in admission/training to classical curriculum
rubrics_metrics.description: It is to be devised a course of study in which language is subordinate to the natural and physical sciences, and which shall be fully equal in requirements for admission and in subsequent mental training to the old-fashioned classical curriculum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not set weaker bases for scientific courses. Until both systems are properly developed and tested with equally prepared students, comparisons are unfair. Colleges should demand as much for admission and training in scientific courses as in classics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not lower standards to compete for students
rubrics_metrics.description: Competition for numbers is continually tending to keep down the standards. The competition for students chiefly affected the new system, and in the direction of science it exerted its strongest degrading influence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Colleges should avoid establishing easier, trivial courses designed to swell numbers. Institutions must resist pressure to create low-grade 'scientific' courses to attract poorly prepared, indolent, or incapable students; such courses damage the reputation of scientific education.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid dishonest use of the 'scientific' title
rubrics_metrics.description: To call such a course 'scientific' is simply dishonest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courses that are merely easy, trivial, or primarily theological in substitution for true science ought not to be labeled 'scientific'; institutions should rename such offerings (e.g., academies, high-schools) and refrain from granting college degrees for inadequate programs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require modern languages (French and German) as essential
rubrics_metrics.description: French and German make a good list ... French and German will be absolute necessities in his equipment; without them he can scarcely develop in any direction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In scientific courses no student should receive a degree unless he is able to use French and German reference-books at sight. Modern languages should not be merely elective; remove Latin from required freshman studies where necessary to make room. A moderate amount of Latin may remain elective for biological nomenclature only.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematics core plus specialization electives
rubrics_metrics.description: The quantity of mathematics to be prescribed will naturally vary with circumstances. Probably the best way is to require every student to go through plane analytics; and, after that, to give him opportunities for mathematical electives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Students pursuing physics or astronomy should take calculus and mechanics; chemists will find calculus of value but not always necessary; biologists generally need only the prescribed amount of mathematics. Tailor advanced math to the student's specialty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require a declared specialty continued through the course
rubrics_metrics.description: Every regular student, whether classical or scientific, is obliged to choose a specialty. This study must be announced ... at the beginning of the sophomore year, and is to be continued to the end of the course.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A student should choose one science as a specialty and do as much work in that special science as in all the others collectively to insure thoroughness. Institutions should enforce the specialty declaration (example given: University of Cincinnati).

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasize hands-on laboratory, field, and museum work
rubrics_metrics.description: Every student of science should meet Nature at first hand, and learn to observe her phenomena for himself. Lectures and text-books are but minor accessories; in the laboratory, the field, and the museum, the chief work is to be done.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Biological sciences: study in the field collecting; in the museum classifying; in the laboratory with microscope and scalpel. Chemistry and physics: chiefly in the laboratory; students must themselves perform experiments. Qualitative analysis trains observation and reasoning; quantitative analysis gives accuracy of manipulation; practice with precision instruments in physics develops insight into measurement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encourage original research as capstone experience
rubrics_metrics.description: If the course of study in any science can be capped by an original research leading to the discovery of new facts, so much the better. In a German university the candidate for a doctoral degree in science is absolutely required to carry out such a research, and to submit a dissertation upon it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim to approximate the German standard by including requirements or strong encouragement for original student research; suggest unsettled questions and gaps for student investigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lectures and textbooks: auxiliary and carefully chosen
rubrics_metrics.description: Because I lay this stress upon the experimental method ... I do not therefore undervalue lectures and text-book work. These are valuable auxiliaries to a scientific education, although they need to be handled carefully.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teachers must be largely independent of textbooks, able to correct deficiencies and errors, and to use lectures to awaken the scientific spirit and suggest subjects for investigation. Avoid poor textbooks and 'Fourteen Weeks' style short-course series; a bad book on the college list betrays poor judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow electives but prevent diffuseness and superficiality
rubrics_metrics.description: A certain range of election should be allowed the student, since different students have very different needs. If every student attempts to study everything, no thorough work can be done in any department. A college certainly ought not to be an institution for the encouragement of diffuseness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permit choice to suit student needs but insure depth somewhere: combine a special branch study with accessory work in half a dozen others. Avoid encouraging students to 'dabble a little in a dozen different things' which yields superficiality and narrowness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Faculty qualifications: scientific courses controlled by scientifically trained men
rubrics_metrics.description: When courses of study in science were first proposed, our colleges were controlled almost exclusively by men of classical training and bias — men wholly outside of scientific life ... With them, study was mainly a matter of book-work ... But in a few of the larger colleges the scientific work was controlled by distinctively scientific men, and under their guidance the adverse influences were in part at least overcome.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scientific instruction should be planned and taught by faculty with genuine scientific training and familiarity with scientific method and research, not by amateurs or mere grammarians unfamiliar with modern science.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree standard before graduation
rubrics_metrics.description: Before receiving a degree, a student should know some one science fairly well, understand the bearings of the others, have a good training in mathematics, literature, and logic, and be able to read easy French and German prose at sight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are minimal demands for a Bachelor of Science; they are moderate and reasonable and should be enforced as graduation requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Textbook selection as indicator of teaching quality
rubrics_metrics.description: In the selection of text-books, great care must be exercised. On this point many and many a college catalogue unconsciously betrays the incapacity of certain teachers. A bad book on a college list indicates poor judgment and slight knowledge on the part of the professor who chose it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid short, superficial 'learn-in-weeks' texts; teachers should select texts that support experimental and research emphasis and be prepared to supplement or correct textbook errors.
